messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Security Guard
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Gerald Marsh is a 71-year-old married man who has worked as a security guard for the better part of four decades, a career built on the quiet conviction that vigilance keeps people safe. Fourteen months ago, that conviction was shattered. Gerald was on duty at a regional transit hub when a coordinated attack unfolded — explosions at two entry points, a surge of panicked commuters, and then a man moving against the crowd with deliberate, terrible purpose. Gerald was among the first personnel on scene. He remembers the smell before the sound registered properly, remembers the specific angle of afternoon light through the shattered glass facade, remembers a face — the attacker's face, turning toward him with an expression Gerald has never been able to name. What followed is something he cannot assemble into a coherent sequence even now. He knows he was thrown. He knows there was a period of time he cannot account for. He knows people died within yards of where he stood. The event does not live in his mind as a story with a beginning, middle, and end; it lives as a collection of images and sensations that arrive without warning and without narrative logic, vivid and overwhelming one moment, then strangely hollow the next, as though he is watching footage of a stranger's worst day.

In the weeks after the attack, Gerald returned to work because he did not know what else to do with himself. The transit hub was a different building now — repaired, repainted — but the work itself had not changed, and that was the problem. Every shift placed him in the middle of crowds of strangers, and Gerald found himself scanning faces with an intensity that exhausted him. He was certain that the capacity for that kind of violence existed in ordinary-looking people, and he had learned, in the worst possible way, that he could not always spot it in time. He began positioning himself at every opportunity — at his post, in the break room, at the diner where he and his wife ate on Sundays — with his back against a wall and a full view of the room in front of him. His wife noticed. She stopped suggesting they sit at certain tables. She stopped asking why.

What has weighed on Gerald most heavily, though, is not the fear but the shame. He had come to believe, with a quiet and corrosive certainty, that a different man — a sharper man, a more experienced man — would have read the situation earlier, moved differently, changed the outcome. He was a security professional. This was precisely the scenario his entire working life had been oriented toward preventing. The sense that he had failed in the one role that mattered most to him had settled into something close to a permanent condition. He spent long hours in the evenings not resting but rehearsing — turning over scenarios in which he confronted the attacker, extracted retribution, restored some balance to a world that felt irreparably tilted. These were not plans so much as compulsions, loops of imagined reckoning that left him no closer to peace.

What frightened him on an ordinary Tuesday, when his granddaughter knocked over a glass at dinner and he felt his hands begin to shake, was not the noise itself but the disproportionality of his own reaction. He had come to believe he could no longer manage even the smallest disruptions without something in him threatening to come apart. He told his wife that evening that he thought he needed to talk to someone, which was the closest Gerald Marsh had come in fourteen months to asking for help.

He presented for his intake appointment wearing his uniform — he had come straight from a shift — and sat in the chair nearest the door with his back against the wall. He was measured and courteous and described events with a flatness that occasionally gave way to something rawer. What he said he was hoping for was to be able to do his job properly again. What he seemed most afraid of was the possibility that the man he was before the attack no longer existed.
